voiceover:
[conversational] That old tool you connected to Gmail might still have access to your inbox.

And stay till the end, because there's one thing removing access does not do.

Founders connect tool after tool, then forget them. Some may be able to read, send or manage your email, and that access stays until you remove it.

Open myaccount.google.com/connections.

Look under "Access to your Google Account". Click an app, then "See details". Don't use it? [confident] Hit "Remove access". Signed in with Google? "Stop using Sign in with Google", then "Confirm".

[serious] Catch: removing a tool you still use can break it, and you could get locked out if Google's its only login.

Then run Security Checkup. Google's 3 steps: devices, old app access, recovery info.

Here's what removal doesn't do. Removal only stops future access, and the app may keep what you already gave it.

How many forgotten apps did you find? Tell me below.

Send this to the friend who clicks Sign in with Google on everything.

Hack saved?

topic: Check which third-party apps and AI tools have access to your Google account or Gmail, and remove the ones you don't use. Open your Google Account's 'Third-party apps & services' page, review each one's access level, revoke the old ones, and run a Security Checkup. Founders connect a lot of tools to Gmail and forget about them.

pick.tool: Google Account > Security > Third-party apps & services
pick.angle: Every tool you ever clicked 'Sign in with Google' on may still be able to read your business inbox. Check it in 60 seconds.
pick.why: 43k views with 1,337 comments is about 3% comments-to-views, a very strong demand signal. It's a checkable, true claim with a real Google page to show on screen. The Gmail storage reel is covered, but this is a different angle. It also fits the recent 'connect ChatGPT to Gmail' content as a security follow-up.

research.tool: Google Account > Security > "Your connections to third-party apps & services" (the "Third-party apps & services" / connections page), plus Google Security Checkup
research.availability: Free for every Google Account. It works on web (myaccount.google.com) and in the Google app on iOS and Android. It is not region-limited or beta. Workspace admins can also control third-party app access for their domain.
steps: Open myaccount.google.com and sign in to the Google account your business uses. Or open Gmail, click your profile picture at the top right, and choose "Manage your Google Account".
Click the "Security" tab. On phone: Android Settings > Google > Manage your Google Account, or iPhone Google app > profile icon > Manage your Google Account, then Security.

Scroll down to "Your connections to third-party apps & services" and click "See all connections". Shortcut: myaccount.google.com/connections. Older links such as /permissions and /linkedapps also redirect to it.

The list is grouped by connection type: "Sign in with Google", "Linked account" and "Access to your Google Account". The last one is the group that can include Gmail, Drive, Calendar or Contacts access.
Click an app, then "See details" to see what it can access.

Remove it with the button that matches the connection type. Sign in with Google: "Stop using Sign in with Google", then "Confirm". Access to your Google Account: "Remove access". Linked account: "Delete link" (some screens say "Delete all connections you have with [app]").

Run the Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup, or search "Security Checkup" while signed in. Google's three-step flow is: review signed-in devices, remove old third-party app access, confirm recovery information.
facts: Google's own post, "See who has access to your Gmail inbox in 2 minutes", recommends three steps: review signed-in devices, remove old third-party app access, and confirm recovery information. It was published about 11 days before today; coverage dates it to October 30.
Google published the blog post on October 30 urging Gmail users to run Security Checkup.
<cite index="2-11,2-12">Linked apps can only access the data and services you authorize. Access levels range from basic account information to viewing or modifying account data.</cite>

<cite index="39-2,39-4">Google's help page says Sign in with Google is for signing in to apps from other developers. To remove the link, select "Stop using Sign in with Google" and then "Confirm".</cite>
<cite index="38-7">If you remove account access, the third-party app may keep info you gave it when you signed in or when you granted extra access.</cite>

<cite index="23-6,23-7,23-8">The connections page has three types: Sign in with Google (apps you signed into), Access to (apps with access to Google services like Drive and Gmail), and Linked account.</cite>
<cite index="42-6,42-7,42-8">Removal options by type: "Stop using Sign in with Google" (after See details), "Remove access" (data access), "Delete link" (linked account).</cite>
<cite index="42-10,42-11">Removing Sign in with Google doesn't delete your account on the third-party service. It only removes Google as the login method.</cite>
<cite index="19-10">You can skip several clicks by going directly to myaccount.google.com/connections.</cite>

<cite index="39-6,39-8">Google's linked-apps help page now also covers AI agents. For example, Gemini can use Sign in with Google to sign into a travel app. Agent permissions appear under "Agents that interact with [app name]" and can be stopped with "Stop using [app name]".</cite>

<cite index="36-6">Reporting on the same Google push says Gmail delegation gives another person direct access to an inbox. It doesn't expire when you change your password and isn't affected by two-factor authentication.</cite> Delegation is a separate setting inside Gmail, not part of the third-party apps page.
do_not_claim: Do NOT say every tool you clicked "Sign in with Google" on can read your inbox. Plain Sign in with Google normally shares basic profile info only. An app can read Gmail only if it was granted a Gmail permission, and it then appears under "Access to your Google Account". Safe wording: "some of them may be able to read, send or manage your email, so check which ones."
Don't say access lasts "forever" or "indefinitely" as a fact. A Facebook-hosted post makes that claim, but it is not a Google source. Say instead that the access stays until you remove it.
Don't promise that revoking deletes your data from the app. Google says the app may keep info you already gave it.

Don't say "Manage third-party access" is the button label. Only some blogs use it (mobileos.it, an unverified blog). Most sources and Google's help use "See all connections". Check the live page before quoting any label.

Don't say the page lists every app. A mobileos.it article says the "Third-party apps & services" page shows only apps that requested specific data permissions, and that you should look for sign-in-only apps separately. Other guides show a Sign in with Google tab on the same page, so this is conflicting. Check the live page.

Don't rely on the caption's "more than you think" as a statistic. There is no transcript or data behind it. Don't invent a count of connected apps. One 2021 arXiv study found 1,010 services using Google SSO and 455 apps using Google APIs across its participants, which is a research sample and not typical.
Don't claim the Security Checkup shows a risk score or malware scan. It is a review of devices, apps and recovery info, and it doesn't detect phishing or deepfake scams (Startup Fortune).
Avoid the smartpartyprep.com claim that the Security Checkup flow is deprecated. Google is actively promoting it as of October 2026.
criticism: Removing access stops future access only. It doesn't delete data the app already copied (Google's help page, scanmyshadow.com).
If you remove Sign in with Google from a tool you still use and it has no password set, you can get locked out of that tool (Neowin). Set another login method first.
Revoking can break integrations such as CRMs, schedulers and email tools that your business relies on, so check what each app does first. This is general advice and not stated by Google.
The Security Checkup doesn't catch AI phishing or deepfake scams, which is the criticism Startup Fortune raised about Google's Oct 30 push.
Some apps will ask for access again the next time you click "Sign in with Google" (a claim from smartpartyprep.com, a low-quality source). Use it as a tip only, not as a fact.

ui.platforms: Web (myaccount.google.com), iOS (Google app) and Android (Settings > Google). The page is responsive, so the desktop and mobile web layouts match.
apps: Gmail web (only as an alternative entry point via profile picture > Manage your Google Account)
screens: Gmail or Google Account home: your profile picture (initial or photo) is at the top right. Click it, then the button "Manage your Google Account".

Google Account home: a left sidebar lists Home, Personal info, Data & privacy, Security, People & sharing, Payments & subscriptions. Click "Security". (Names and order may vary slightly, so check the live page.)

Security page: cards run down the page, including "Recent security activity", "How you sign in to Google", "Your devices" and "Your connections to third-party apps & services". The last card shows the first few connected apps with their logos and a "See all connections" link at the bottom. On phone, scroll to the same card.

Connections page: filter chips or tabs read "Sign in with Google", "Access to your Google Account" and "Linked account". Each row shows the app name and logo, and the Gmail, Drive or Contacts permission. Tap a row to open it. Default theme follows the device (light by default; a Neowin screenshot shows dark mode).

App detail page: sections show what the app can access and the connection type. There is a "See details" button, and then one of the buttons "Stop using Sign in with Google", "Remove access", "Delete link" or "Delete all connections you have with [app]".
Confirmation dialog: a "Confirm" button (or OK on older flows) finishes the removal. The app then disappears from the list.

Security Checkup page: a list of items such as Your devices, Recent security activity, Sign-in & recovery, Third-party access and Your saved passwords. Each row can be expanded with a down arrow, and Third-party access has an "i" info icon and "Remove access". A green shield shows when everything is fine.

research.visuals: Only a real screen recording of the signed-in Google Account page can show the user's actual connected-app list, and it will contain personal data to blur. For generic visuals, use the public help article (it has product screenshots) and the Google blog post. Show the Security tab, the "Your connections to third-party apps & services" card, the Sign in with Google / Access to your Google Account groups, and the "Remove access" or "Stop using Sign in with Google" button. The end result is the app disappearing from the list.

research.notes: Verdict is "adjust" because the trick works and Google is promoting it right now, but the angle overclaims. Rewrite it as "Some tools you connected may still be able to read or send your email" and not "every Sign in with Google tool can read your inbox". Timeliness hook: Google's official post "See who has access to your Gmail inbox in 2 minutes" ran on October 30, 2026. Naming: Google's UI says "Your connections to third-party apps & services" on the Security page, and its help articles say "third-party connections" and "linked apps". The Yahoo/How-To Geek path (Data & privacy > Third-party apps & services) is also reported, so both entry paths probably exist. The 60-second claim is roughly right; Google says 2 minutes for the full three-step checkup, so say "a minute or two". The popular reel has no transcript, so there are no transcript claims to check. Its caption ("more than you think") is vague and unverifiable. I couldn't open myaccount.google.com or the Google help pages directly, so exact on-screen labels come from Google's help snippets and third-party walkthroughs. Do a quick live check of label wording and position before recording.
